newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-CRUDE RISE IN APIS REFLECTS SLOWING DEMAND.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CRUDE RISE IN APIS REFLECTS SLOWING DEMAND.

text.p: The surprising rise in U.S. crude oil inventories last week reflects refineries scaling back consumption in anticipation of the end driving season early next month, analysts said Tuesday.
The 2.7 million barrel increase in nationwide crude oil stocks reported by the American Petroleum Institute (API) came as refinery utilization dipped 2.1 percentage points to 95 percent of capacity.

Strangely, gasoline output rose 144,000 barrels per day (bpd). But analysts explained that refiners have begun to throttle back use of crude oil and are using up gasoline blending components to bulk up their output of gasoline.
"It's not unusal for this time of year," Ken Miller, senior analyst at Purvin and Gertz Inc in Houston, said.
"Refineries will try to work down inventories of (blending components)," he said, citing a sharp three million barrel, or 400,000 bpd, draw in gasoline blending components last week.
At the same, refineries scaled back crude runs to 14.68 million bpd from 15 million the previous week.
But some analysts attributed the 2.1 percentage point drop in refinery use to delayed reporting of shutdowns at huge New Jersey refineries owned by Tosco and Exxon.
Meanwhile, crude imports continued to pour in the U.S. at a rate of nine million bpd, leading some market observers to conclude that refinery use could rise slightly next week.
"We are still in the heart of vacation demand season. We should even start to see draws for Labor Day this week and next," said Peter Beutel, president of Cameron Hanover.
Gasoline stocks stood at 191,062 million barrels, down what analysts called a "neutral" 863,000 barrels from the week before.
Implied gasoine demand, which had averaged about 8.6 million barrels to August 1, eased to 8.24 million barrels for the week ending August 8, analysts said.
Meanwhile, distillates showed a "bullish" decline of 745,000 barrels last week as harvests around the country increased diesel fuel demand from farmers.
